findings.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — [advisory, confidence=100, P2] `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, resource -> {` invokes `hasGrantedPermission(resource, scope)` for every stored client resource and accumulates every grant before returning, so callers pay an unbounded full-realm authorization scan as fine-grained client grants grow; although the callback avoids initially materializing every resource, it neither bounds policy evaluations nor the returned set, and a paginated or candidate-ID-scoped lookup removes those unnecessary evaluations.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:224 — [advisory, confidence=100, P3] `Collection<Permission> permissions = root.evaluatePermission(new ResourcePermission(resource, resource.getScopes(), server), server);` duplicates the evaluation-and-scope-match algorithm at lines 249 and 276, forcing the next evaluation or scope-matching fix to update three implementations; although client-specific and all-client resource resolution differ, both already resolve a Resource before this identical operation, so routing both through the existing hasGrantedPermission helper deletes two evaluation loops and two singleton expectedScopes lists without combining their distinct lookup rules.

server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/AdminPermissionsSchema.java:68 — [confidence=75, P1] Adding `public static final ResourceType CLIENTS = new ResourceType(CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, Set.of(CONFIGURE, MANAGE, MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE, VIEW));` leaves existing V2-enabled realms without the Clients resource and new scopes because `init` returns immediately for an existing admin-permissions client at lines 226–228, so those administrators cannot create configure or client-role-mapping permissions after upgrading because `getScope` rejects the absent scopes.

goldens.comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that getClientsWithPermission() iterates over all client resources via resourceStore.findByType() and calls hasGrantedPermission() for each one, accumulating results in a HashSet without any pagination or bounds. This is a legitimate scalability/performance concern for realms with many clients. However, this is not a bug (the code functions correctly) but rather an architectural concern about the new implementation's performance characteristics at scale. The diff clearly shows this pattern at lines 131-140 of ClientPermissionsV2.java.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that lines 224, 249, and 276 in ClientPermissionsV2.java contain nearly identical code patterns for evaluating permissions and checking scopes. Looking at the diff: hasPermission(ClientModel, String) at ~line 224 creates ResourcePermission, calls evaluatePermission, and loops through permissions checking scopes. hasPermission(String) at ~line 249 does the same. hasGrantedPermission at ~line 276 also does the same loop. The suggestion to consolidate these into the hasGrantedPermission helper is a valid refactoring concern - the code duplication means any fix to the evaluation logic would need to be applied in multiple places. This is a legitimate maintainability/architecture concern introduced by this diff, not a bug or hallucination.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real migration issue. Looking at the diff, new scopes (CONFIGURE, MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE) and a new CLIENTS resource type are added to AdminPermissionsSchema. The finding claims that existing V2-enabled realms won't get these new resources/scopes because the init method returns early for existing admin-permissions clients. While the diff doesn't show the init method directly, this is a valid concern for schema migrations - the new CLIENTS ResourceType and its scopes are defined statically, but existing realms that already have the admin-permissions client initialized would not automatically receive these new schema elements. This would prevent administrators from creating permissions using the new scopes after upgrading.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:78 — confidence=100 P1: `if (canView() || canConfigure(client)) {` returns true for an all-clients VIEW grant before evaluating the target client resource, so an administrator explicitly denied VIEW on a particular client still reads that client and its configuration because `canView()` evaluates only the global Clients resource.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a logic issue in ClientPermissionsV2.canView(ClientModel client) at line 78. The method checks `if (canView() || canConfigure(client))` where canView() (line 85-87) checks for global VIEW permission on all clients. This means if a user has VIEW permission on the 'Clients' resource type (all clients), they can view ANY specific client, even if there's a specific deny permission on that particular client. The method should check client-specific permissions before falling back to global permissions, similar to how canManage(ClientModel client) works - it checks the admin role first, then checks hasPermission(client, MANAGE) for the specific client. This is a real authorization bypass bug where deny permissions on specific clients are ineffective when a global VIEW grant exists.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test `testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient` grants multiple scopes together (MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE, CONFIGURE) in a single permission, which means the test doesn't verify that each scope is independently required for its respective operation. Looking at the diff, the test creates one permission with all three scopes and then tests both `roles().clientLevel().add()` and `roles().get().addComposites()` operations. If the implementation incorrectly checked MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE instead of MAP_ROLES (or vice versa), this test would still pass because both scopes are granted. This is a valid test coverage concern - the test should ideally verify each scope independently to catch implementation bugs where scope checks are swapped.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test `testViewAllClients()` uses `assertThat(found, not(empty()))` which only verifies that at least one client is returned, not that ALL clients are visible. Looking at the diff, the test creates an 'all-clients' VIEW permission and then asserts the result is 'not empty'. A more robust test would compare against the actual count of clients in the realm to verify the 'all-clients' behavior works correctly. This is a valid test coverage concern - the test doesn't fully verify the advertised 'all-clients' functionality, though it does verify the permission changes access (from empty to non-empty).
